query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The onset and progression of the phase transition in solid FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles is governed by defect-induced surface premelting. Specifically, rapid Joule heating generates a high density of surface defects that serve as nucleation sites for a transient liquid-like layer, which then propagates inward to enable the melting transition.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, disordered, solid-solution FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with a relatively uniform composition.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid Joule heating (with precise temperature and time control) to drive the nanoparticles into the premelting/melting regime, followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Heating to temperatures just above the solid-state stability limit (near the nanoparticle melting threshold) in an inert atmosphere, with controlled heating durations (tens of milliseconds to minutes) and subsequent rapid cooling (order of 10^4 K/s). A controlled comparison would involve performing identical heating experiments with varied heating rates or pre-annealing steps to reduce native defect density.
generation.structural_mediator: The surface defect density (especially at the nanoparticle edge or surface irregularities) that evolves during rapid Joule heating, which mediates the initial nucleation of a liquid-like layer.
generation.mechanism: Rapid Joule heating induces high thermal gradients and stresses in the nanoparticle, which creates numerous atomic-scale defects at the surface. These defects lower the local melting barrier and cause a thin, liquid-like layer to form (premelting) at the surface. As heating continues, these liquid regions coalesce and propagate inward, leading to complete melting. The subsequent rapid quenching freezes in the intermediate structures, making the process experimentally observable.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under rapid Joule heating, one should observe the formation of a liquid-like layer at the nanoparticle surfaces prior to full melting. Compared to a baseline of uniformly heated nanoparticles (or nanoparticles pre-annealed to reduce defects), nanoparticles with a higher initial defect density will exhibit a lower onset temperature for premelting and a faster progression to complete melting.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles heated under conditions that minimize defect formation (or with a pre-treated, lower-defect surface), which would display a higher and more uniform melting onset without marked surface premelting.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to dominate in the premelting and melting regime under rapid heating conditions. It may not apply if the heating rates are slow enough to allow for equilibrium defect annealing or if external effects (such as interactions with substrates) significantly alter the defect dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relation between defect density and the drop in the local melting point is not well established, and the role of potential elemental segregation at the defect sites remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles. One set will be produced with standard rapid Joule heating to induce high defect densities, while the other set is pre-annealed at a lower temperature to reduce surface defects before identical Joule heating. Use in situ TEM to monitor the onset and progression of melting.
measurements: High-resolution TEM imaging of surface structure to quantify defect density and observe the formation of liquid-like layers.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect changes in melting onset temperature.
Time-resolved diffraction or spectroscopic measurements to track phase changes during heating.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of nanoparticles — regardless of their initial defect density — exhibit essentially the same premelting onset temperature and progression behavior, then the hypothesis that surface defects govern the melting transition will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.

cited_evidence.text: In order to rule out the effect of electromigration on the formation of nanoparticles, rapid radiative heating process was used to synthesize nanoparticles on carbon support. The rapid radiative heating setup is schematically shown in Fig. S5a. In this configuration, the outside carbon film acts as a source for flash high temperature radiation to heat up the S-CNF. At this condition, the salt-loaded CNFs were only exposed to high temperatures under ultrafast heating rate (>105 K/s), and no direct electrical current was applied to the S-CNFs. After rapid radiative heating treatment, the prepared Pt NPs@CNF specimens were analyzed via HRSTEM. As we can see from Fig. S5b, a uniform distribution of small nanoparticles was observed on the CNF support. Similar to the Joule heating case, the amorphous carbon film showed evidence of crystallization and the NPs were associated with the T-graphite edge planes. To summarize, we included the above experiments in Table S1. Overall, it is evident that the formation and stabilization of nanoparticles are governed by the rapid heating process, and not necessarily electromigration. To synthesize the MPEI nanoparticles, we preloaded a carbon substrate with desired metal salt precursor combinations/ratios and Joule-heated (fig. S5) the materials with precise control of the temperature and heating/cooling rates by tuning the power applied to the substrate (fig. S6). The temperature profile and structural evolution of nanoparticles over time are illustrated in Fig. 2A. We first synthesize solid-solution (HEA) nanoparticles () by heating the metal precursors for tens of milliseconds at ~1100 K. This is a critical step for mixing the different elements without phase separation. A disorder-to-order phase transition is then achieved by rapidly reheating the materials to ~1100 K for an additional ~5 min—a limited amount of time that is sufficient to complete the desired transition from the disordered HEA structure to the ordered, single-phase MPEI configuration while simultaneously avoiding nanoparticle growth/agglomeration. Last, the single-phase MPEI structure and small particle size (~5 nm) is preserved by rapidly cooling the materials (~104 K/s).

chosen.approach: Joule heating synthesis with rapid quenching of nanoparticles
